question: A child builds towers using identically shaped cubes of different colors. How many different towers with a height \(8\) cubes can the child build with \(2\) red cubes, \(3\) blue cubes, and \(4\) green cubes? (One cube will be left out.)
solution:
A tower is determined by its colors from bottom to top. Since exactly one cube is unused, its color gives three cases.

For a fixed collection of \(r\) red, \(b\) blue, and \(g\) green cubes totaling \(8\), temporarily labeling all cubes gives \(8!\) orders. Each color pattern is counted \(r!b!g!\) times by exchanging labels among cubes of the same color. Thus the number of different towers is
\[
\frac{8!}{r!b!g!}.
\]
Applying this to each possible unused color gives:

| Unused color | Cubes used | Number of towers |
|---|---|---:|
| Red | \(1\) red, \(3\) blue, \(4\) green | \(\dfrac{8!}{1!3!4!}=280\) |
| Blue | \(2\) red, \(2\) blue, \(4\) green | \(\dfrac{8!}{2!2!4!}=420\) |
| Green | \(2\) red, \(3\) blue, \(3\) green | \(\dfrac{8!}{2!3!3!}=560\) |

Every tower belongs to exactly one row because its color counts determine the unused color. Therefore the total is
\[
280+420+560=\boxed{1260},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
